subject: chemistry
title: Chemical bonding
summary: Covers ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, Lewis structures, formal charge, resonance, bond energies and lengths, electronegativity and bond polarity, and introduces valence bond theory and sp, sp² and sp³ hybridisation.
body:
A **chemical bond** is a lasting attraction between atoms that lowers the total energy of the system. The type of bonding in a substance, whether ionic, covalent or metallic, controls its melting point, conductivity, hardness and reactivity. This lesson revises the three bonding types in more depth than VCE, then uses Lewis structures, formal charge, resonance and bond energies to describe covalent molecules, and introduces valence bond theory and hybridisation to explain how covalent bonds form from orbitals.

## Key ideas

### Ionic bonding

**Ionic bonding** is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice. It forms when electrons are transferred from an element with low ionisation energy (a metal) to one with high electron affinity (a non-metal). Forming the ions actually costs energy overall; the payoff is the very large energy released when gaseous ions come together into a lattice. This is measured by the **lattice energy**. By Coulomb's law the attraction is proportional to q₁q₂/r, where q is ion charge and r is the distance between ion centres. So lattice energy increases with higher ionic charge and smaller ions. That is why MgO (2+ and 2− ions) melts at about 2850 °C while NaCl (1+ and 1−) melts at 801 °C.

### Metallic bonding

**Metallic bonding** is the attraction between a lattice of metal cations and a "sea" of **delocalised** valence electrons that move freely through the whole structure. Delocalised electrons explain electrical and thermal conductivity, and because the bonding is not directional, layers of cations can slide without breaking the structure, which makes metals malleable and ductile.

### Covalent bonding and Lewis structures

A **covalent bond** is a shared pair of electrons attracted to two nuclei. It forms between non-metals, where neither atom can easily lose electrons. A **Lewis structure** shows all valence electrons as bonding pairs (lines) and **lone pairs** (dots). A reliable method:

1. Count total valence electrons (add one for each negative charge, subtract one for each positive charge).
2. Choose the central atom, usually the least electronegative atom (never H), and connect all atoms with single bonds.
3. Complete octets on the outer atoms with lone pairs.
4. Place any remaining electrons on the central atom.
5. If the central atom has fewer than eight electrons, turn lone pairs on outer atoms into multiple bonds.

Exceptions to the octet rule include **electron-deficient** molecules such as BF₃ (boron has only six electrons), odd-electron molecules (**radicals**) such as NO, and **expanded octets** for elements in period 3 and below, such as PCl₅ (10 electrons on P) and SF₆ (12 on S).

### Formal charge

When more than one Lewis structure is possible, **formal charge** helps pick the best one. It is the charge an atom would have if every bonding pair were shared equally:

`formal charge = (valence electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons)`

The sum of formal charges equals the overall charge of the species. The preferred structure has formal charges as close to zero as possible, and any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom.

### Resonance

Some species cannot be described by a single Lewis structure. In the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, one double bond and two single bonds can be drawn in three equivalent ways. These are **resonance structures**, joined by a double-headed arrow. The real ion is a **resonance hybrid**, a single structure in which the π electrons are delocalised over all three N–O bonds. All three bonds are identical in length, with a **bond order** of 4/3 (4 bonding pairs shared over 3 bonds). The ion does not flip between structures. Benzene is the classic example: all six C–C bonds are 139 pm, between a C–C single bond (154 pm) and a C=C double bond (134 pm), with bond order 1.5.

### Bond energies and bond lengths

**Bond energy** (bond dissociation enthalpy) is the energy needed to break one mole of a given bond in gaseous molecules, for example `H₂(g) → 2H(g)   ΔH = +436 kJ mol⁻¹`. Tabulated values for bonds such as C–H are averages over many compounds. As bond order increases between the same two atoms, bonds get shorter and stronger:

| Bond | Length (pm) | Average bond energy (kJ mol⁻¹) |
|---|---|---|
| C–C | 154 | 346 |
| C=C | 134 | 614 |
| C≡C | 120 | 839 |

Since breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it, the enthalpy change of a gas-phase reaction can be estimated as

`ΔH ≈ Σ (bond energies of bonds broken) − Σ (bond energies of bonds formed)`

The estimate is approximate because average values are used and all species must be gases.

### Electronegativity and bond polarity

**Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electrons towards itself (Pauling scale: F 4.0, O 3.4, N 3.0, Cl 3.2, C 2.6, H 2.2, Na 0.9). When two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity, the electrons are shared unequally, giving a **polar covalent bond** with partial charges, δ+ and δ−. Bonding is best seen as a continuum: a difference near 0 gives a non-polar covalent bond, a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond, and a large difference (roughly above 1.8–2.0) gives mainly ionic bonding. No bond is 100% ionic.

### Valence bond theory and hybridisation

**Valence bond theory** says a covalent bond forms when an orbital on one atom **overlaps** with an orbital on another, and the two electrons in the overlap region are attracted to both nuclei. Greater overlap means a stronger bond. Head-on overlap along the line between the nuclei gives a **sigma (σ) bond**. Side-on overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below that line, gives a **pi (π) bond**. A single bond is one σ bond; a double bond is one σ and one π; a triple bond is one σ and two π. π bonds prevent rotation about the bond axis, which is why cis and trans isomers of alkenes exist.

A problem arises with carbon. Its ground state is 2s² 2p², which has only two unpaired electrons, yet carbon in CH₄ forms four identical bonds at 109.5°. The solution is **hybridisation**: atomic orbitals on the same atom mix to form an equal number of new, equivalent **hybrid orbitals** pointed in the directions the bonds actually take.

| Hybridisation | Orbitals mixed | Hybrid orbitals | Geometry | Angle | Unhybridised p orbitals | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sp³ | one s + three p | 4 | tetrahedral | 109.5° | 0 | CH₄, NH₃, H₂O |
| sp² | one s + two p | 3 | trigonal planar | 120° | 1 | C₂H₄, BF₃ |
| sp | one s + one p | 2 | linear | 180° | 2 | C₂H₂, CO₂ |

To find an atom's hybridisation, count its **electron domains** (bonded atoms plus lone pairs; a multiple bond counts as one domain): 4 domains = sp³, 3 = sp², 2 = sp. Hybrid orbitals form σ bonds or hold lone pairs; the leftover unhybridised p orbitals form π bonds. In ethene, each C is sp²; the C–C σ bond comes from sp²–sp² overlap and the π bond from side-on overlap of the two unhybridised 2p orbitals.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: choosing a structure with formal charge

Compare H–C≡N and H–N≡C (each has 10 valence electrons and a lone pair on the terminal atom).

In H–C≡N:
- C: 4 − 0 − ½(8) = 0
- N: 5 − 2 − ½(6) = 0
- H: 1 − 0 − ½(2) = 0

In H–N≡C:
- N: 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1
- C: 4 − 2 − ½(6) = −1

H–C≡N has all formal charges zero, so it is the preferred structure, matching the known structure of hydrogen cyanide.

### Example 2: estimating ΔH from bond energies

Estimate ΔH for `CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)` using C–H 414, O=O 498, C=O 804 and O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹.

1. Bonds broken: 4 C–H + 2 O=O = 4(414) + 2(498) = 1656 + 996 = 2652 kJ mol⁻¹
2. Bonds formed: 2 C=O + 4 O–H = 2(804) + 4(463) = 1608 + 1852 = 3460 kJ mol⁻¹
3. ΔH ≈ 2652 − 3460 = **−808 kJ mol⁻¹** (3 significant figures: −8.08 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹)

This is close to the experimental value of about −802 kJ mol⁻¹; the small difference comes from using average bond energies.

### Example 3: σ bonds, π bonds and hybridisation in acetonitrile, CH₃CN

1. Bonds: three C–H single bonds, one C–C single bond and one C≡N triple bond.
2. σ bonds: 3 + 1 + 1 = **5**. π bonds: 2 (both in C≡N).
3. The CH₃ carbon has 4 domains, so sp³. The nitrile carbon has 2 domains (C–C and C≡N), so sp, and the C–C≡N unit is linear.

## Common mistakes

- Treating resonance structures as different molecules that switch back and forth. There is one real structure, the hybrid.
- Confusing formal charge with oxidation number. Formal charge shares bonding electrons equally; oxidation number gives them all to the more electronegative atom.
- Reversing the bond energy formula. It is bonds broken minus bonds formed, the opposite way round from ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
- Counting a double bond as two electron domains when assigning hybridisation. A multiple bond is one domain.
- Saying a double bond is "twice as strong" as a single bond. A π bond is weaker than a σ bond, so C=C (614) is less than 2 × C–C (692).

## Exam tips

- Lewis structures earn marks only if every lone pair is shown and the total electron count is correct. Count electrons at the end as a check.
- When asked to "justify" a structure, quote calculated formal charges for each atom.
- Hybridisation answers should name the hybridisation, the electron domain geometry and the bond angle, and identify which orbitals overlap to form each σ and π bond.
- Bond energy calculations are often followed by "why does this differ from the experimental value?". Answer: average bond energies, and the method assumes all species are gases.

## Tips to remember

- **Three bonds, three pictures.** Ionic = a tug-of-war already won (electrons transferred, ions held in a lattice); covalent = a shared pair held by two nuclei; metallic = cations floating in a "sea" of delocalised electrons. Ask "transferred, shared or pooled?" to classify any substance.
- **Lattice energy follows Coulomb: "big charge, small ions, strong lattice."** Attraction ∝ q₁q₂/r, so doubling both charges makes MgO melt at about 2850 °C versus 801 °C for NaCl.
- **Formal charge in one line:** FC = valence − dots − ½ × bonding electrons (made-up memory phrase: "*what it owns, minus what it keeps, minus half of what it shares*"). Best structure: charges near zero, any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
- **Resonance is a mule, not a flip-flop.** A mule is not a horse one moment and a donkey the next — it is always a blend. Likewise NO₃⁻ is always the hybrid, with every N–O bond order 4/3.
- **"Break minus make."** ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Breaking costs energy, making pays it back — the opposite order to H(products) − H(reactants).
- **Count domains to get hybridisation: 4 → sp³ (109.5°), 3 → sp² (120°), 2 → sp (180°).** The superscripts add up to the number of domains (sp³ = 1 + 3 = 4), and a multiple bond counts as one domain. Every bond has one σ; each extra bond in a double or triple is a π from leftover p orbitals.

## Key terms

- **Lattice energy** — the energy released when one mole of an ionic solid forms from its gaseous ions.
- **Delocalised electrons** — electrons not confined to one bond or atom, spread over several atoms.
- **Lewis structure** — a diagram showing bonding pairs and lone pairs of valence electrons.
- **Formal charge** — valence electrons minus non-bonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons.
- **Resonance hybrid** — the real structure of a species described by two or more resonance structures.
- **Bond order** — the number of electron pairs shared between two atoms (may be fractional in a hybrid).
- **Bond energy** — the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in the gas phase.
- **Electronegativity** — an atom's ability to attract bonding electrons towards itself.
- **Sigma (σ) bond** — a bond formed by head-on orbital overlap along the internuclear axis.
- **Pi (π) bond** — a bond formed by side-on overlap of parallel p orbitals.
- **Hybridisation** — the mixing of atomic orbitals on one atom to form equivalent hybrid orbitals.

## Summary

- Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction in a lattice; lattice energy grows with ion charge and falls with ion size. Metallic bonding is cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.
- Lewis structures are built by counting valence electrons; formal charge picks the best structure, and resonance describes delocalised electrons.
- Higher bond order means shorter, stronger bonds; ΔH ≈ bonds broken − bonds formed.
- Electronegativity differences make bonds polar; bonding is a continuum from non-polar covalent to ionic.
- Valence bond theory forms bonds by orbital overlap: σ bonds head-on, π bonds side-on.
- sp³, sp² and sp hybrids give tetrahedral, trigonal planar and linear arrangements, decided by counting electron domains.

questions.prompt: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethyne, HC≡CH?
questions.explanation: Each carbon has two electron domains (one C–H and one C≡C, which counts as a single domain), so it is sp hybridised and linear, with two unhybridised p orbitals forming the two π bonds. Option B is tempting if you count the triple bond as more than one domain, or confuse ethyne with ethene.

questions.prompt: Which ionic compound would be expected to have the largest lattice energy?
questions.explanation: Lattice energy is proportional to q₁q₂/r. MgO and CaO both have 2+ and 2− ions (four times the charge product of NaCl or KBr), and Mg²⁺ is smaller than Ca²⁺, so MgO has the shortest ion separation and largest lattice energy. Option C is tempting because it has the same charges, but Ca²⁺ is larger.

questions.prompt: In the preferred Lewis structure of the thiocyanate ion, [S=C=N]⁻, sulfur has two lone pairs and nitrogen has two lone pairs. What are the formal charges on S, C and N respectively?
questions.explanation: S: 6 − 4 − ½(4) = 0. C: 4 − 0 − ½(8) = 0. N: 5 − 4 − ½(4) = −1. The sum is −1, matching the ion's charge, and the negative charge sits on N, the more electronegative of S and N. Option B places the charge on sulfur, which does not match the electron counts given.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, is correct?

options.A: It has one C=O bond that is shorter than the two C–O bonds.
options.B: It rapidly alternates between three different structures.
options.C: All three C–O bonds are identical, with a bond order of 4/3.
options.D: All three C–O bonds are double bonds.

questions.explanation: Carbonate is a resonance hybrid of three equivalent structures; the π electron pair is delocalised over all three bonds, so they are equal in length with bond order (1 + 1 + 2)/3 = 4/3. Option B is the classic misconception: resonance structures are not real species that interconvert.

questions.prompt: Use the average bond energies H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242 and H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹ to estimate ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
questions.explanation: Bonds broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ mol⁻¹. Bonds formed: 2 × 432 = 864 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH ≈ 678 − 864 = −186 kJ mol⁻¹. Option A has the right size but the wrong sign, from calculating bonds formed minus bonds broken. Options C and D (±246) come from forgetting that two H–Cl bonds form.

questions.prompt: How many σ bonds and π bonds are present in a molecule of propenal, CH₂=CH–CHO?
questions.explanation: Bonds: four C–H, one C=C, one C–C and one C=O. Every bond contains one σ bond, giving 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7 σ. Each double bond adds one π, giving 2 π. Option B (9 σ) counts each double bond as two σ bonds; option A forgets some C–H bonds.

questions.prompt: In valence bond theory, which orbitals overlap to form the π bond in ethene, C₂H₄?

options.A: An unhybridised 2p orbital on each carbon, overlapping side-on
options.B: An sp² orbital on each carbon, overlapping head-on
options.C: An sp² orbital on one carbon and a 1s orbital on hydrogen
options.D: An sp³ orbital on each carbon, overlapping side-on

questions.explanation: Each sp² carbon keeps one unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane; these overlap side-on to form the π bond. Option B describes the C–C σ bond, and option C describes the C–H σ bonds. The carbons in ethene are sp², not sp³.

questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules contains a central atom that does NOT obey the octet rule because it has fewer than eight valence electrons?
questions.explanation: Boron has three valence electrons and forms three single bonds, giving only six electrons around it: it is electron deficient. Option C is tempting because PCl₅ also breaks the octet rule, but P has ten electrons (an expanded octet), not fewer than eight.
